7.1 — Tilemaps: The Level Editor

Dragging platform sprites one by one is a hobby; painting levels on a grid is an editor. Today you set up the Tilemap — the tool that makes a cave the size of a cave buildable in an hour — and learn why every level you love was drawn, not placed.

Build Lab ~15 min

Step 1 — the grid. In the Platformer scene: GameObject → 2D Object → Tilemap → Rectangular. You get a Grid parent and a Tilemap child. Everything snaps to the Grid's cell size (default 1×1 — and your sprites are scaled to match, which is why the starter art fits).

Step 2 — the palette. Window → 2D → Tile Palette. Create a new palette (save it in Assets/Tilemaps/Palettes), then drag the starter's tile sprites (look in Assets/Sprites for the cave/platformer ground and wall pieces) into the palette window. Unity slices each into a Tile. Now you have a paint tray.

Step 3 — the tools. With the Tilemap child selected: Paint (drag), Rect (fill), Erase, Eye Dropper (grab the tile under the cursor), Fill (flood). Draw a floor the whole width of the camera, a wall, and a small raised ledge. If painting does not appear: check the Tilemap child is selected, not the Grid parent — the classic first-15-minutes bug.

Step 4 — the scale question. Your gauntlet from 6.5 used loose platforms. Redraw its five sections on the tilemap grid. Where the geometry fights the grid (a gap that is 1.5 tiles), you now have a DECISION: change the gap or change the grid. Always change the gap — the grid is a contract with every other system (colliders, turrets, snap spawns).

Bug Hunt: Editor bugs

  1. Paint a tile, press Play, unpaint it — did your edit survive? Why does the Scene (data file!) reload on Play, and what does that mean for "save before test" as a religion?
  2. Paint on the Grid parent's own Tilemap vs a second Tilemap child. Why will collision layers (7.2) want SEPARATE tilemaps for ground vs. decoration?
  3. Zoom way in and paint a tile partially off-grid. What does the editor REFUSE to let you do — and why is that refusal the whole point of a grid?
Design Lab ~20 min

An editor changes how you think. With loose sprites you were placing; on a grid you are drawing. Do this now, on paper first, 30 seconds each, then paint the winner:

  1. A "teeth" jump: two platforms, one gap, spikes below — the smallest sentence in platformer grammar
  2. A "stair" — three ledges each one tile higher. Where does the player look while climbing — and where should the NEXT threat be visible from?
  3. A "room" — an enclosed space with exactly two exits, one at floor level and one you must jump UP to reach. This is the boss arena seed for Unit 8

Socratic

The AP exam describes a data abstraction as hiding implementation behind a representation. A tilemap IS your level stored as a grid of numbers. What does the paint tool hide — and what would you lose if you edited the numbers directly?

Tinker: Editor craft

  1. Build one 10-tile "language" of shapes (gap, stair, teeth, room, corridor) and reuse each at least twice in different sizes. Why do real level designers work in reusable phrases rather than one-off layouts?
  2. Decorate: can you paint BACKGROUND tiles on a second tilemap with no collider — what makes them different from ground (hint: that is 7.2a's whole lesson)?

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Create a tilemap + palette and paint/erase/rect/fill with confidence
  • Explain grid-snap as a contract with the rest of the game
  • Sketch then build the three core shapes: teeth, stair, room
  • Explain "drawing, not placing" — the editor mindset shift
